sysd-found-049.title: Transport Layer Security: three jobs in one protocol
sysd-found-049.text:
TLS does three jobs at once. Encryption hides the data from third parties. A check of identity ensures the parties are who they claim to be. An integrity check verifies the data has not been forged or tampered with. Transport Layer Security is a cryptographic protocol that provides secured communications over a computer network, giving applications privacy, integrity and authenticity.

It is used in email and voice over IP, but securing {{ref:sysd-found-048}} is its most visible use. TLS evolved from {{ref:sysd-found-046}} and is an IETF standard first defined in 1999. The current version is {{ref:sysd-found-188}}, defined in August 2018. It is made of two layers, the record protocol and the handshake protocol, and runs on top of a reliable transport such as TCP.

Applications can run with or without TLS, so the client must ask the server for a TLS connection. It does so either with a separate port, 443 for secured web traffic rather than 80 for HTTP, or with a protocol-specific STARTTLS request. The handshake uses an asymmetric cipher to set the cipher parameters and a session-specific shared key, and further communication is encrypted with a symmetric cipher. That key is unique to each connection and negotiated at the start, which keeps the connection private. Public-key cryptography proves identity, required for the server and optional for the client. Each message carries a check code, so lost or altered data is detected.

sysd-found-048.title: HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel
sysd-found-048.text:
Plain HTTP is not encrypted, so it is open to eavesdropping and to a {{ref:sysd-found-179}}. Those attacks expose accounts and sensitive information or inject malware and advertisements into pages. HTTPS is designed to withstand them. It is HTTP carried over an encrypted TLS connection, so web traffic is private, authenticated and protected from tampering in transit. The main motivations are proof that the website is the one requested and protection of the privacy and integrity of exchanged data.

HTTPS is not a separate protocol but ordinary HTTP over an encrypted SSL/TLS connection. Its URLs begin with https:// and use port 443 by default, while HTTP uses port 80. Because HTTP runs entirely on top of TLS, the URL, query parameters, headers, cookies and message data can all be encrypted.

Usually only the server is verified, by the client examining its certificate, which a trusted third party must sign. TLS still protects the channel when only one side is verified. It typically uses long-term public and private keys to generate a short-term session key that encrypts the data flow. A hijacker of the traffic gets only binary data. For HTTPS to be effective a whole site must be served over it. Loading scripts or images over HTTP, or only a login page over HTTPS, leaves users open to attacks and surveillance. Deploying HTTPS also allows HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, which are designed to reduce page load times, size and latency.

sysd-found-179.title: Man-in-the-middle attacks: the eavesdropper who relays everything
sysd-found-179.text: The attacker does not need to break any encryption. A man-in-the-middle attack, or on-path attack, is one where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are talking directly. In active eavesdropping the attacker makes independent connections with both victims and relays messages, controlling the whole conversation. That means intercepting all relevant messages and injecting new ones, which is easy near an unencrypted Wi-Fi access point. With public keys it goes like this. Mallory replaces Bob's public key with her own, so Alice encrypts to Mallory. Mallory decrypts, reads or alters the message and re-encrypts it with Bob's key. The parties need a way to know they hold real keys. Variants include HTTPS spoofing with a fake certificate, SSL/TLS stripping that downgrades HTTPS to HTTP, evil-twin Wi-Fi and certificates signed by a fraudulent CA. The defenses are identity checks and tamper detection. TLS verifies one or both parties through a mutually trusted certificate authority, but most connections verify only the server, so these attacks can still occur.

sysd-found-169.title: Securing cookies against theft, scripts and forgery
sysd-found-169.text: Steal a user's cookies and, to most servers, you are that user. Most sites use cookies as the only identifier of a user session. An attacker who steals a victim's full set of cookies is therefore treated by the server as the victim's session. Securing cookies means protecting those identifiers from theft and misuse. Cookies sent over unencrypted HTTP can be read by anyone on the network, such as on open Wi-Fi. TLS fixes this, and the Secure attribute makes the browser send the cookie only over an encrypted channel. Attackers can also steal cookies with {{ref:sysd-reliab-127}}, by getting their JavaScript to send document.cookie to them. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by client-side scripts, which mitigates this. A second danger is {{ref:sysd-reliab-129}}, which abuses automatic cookie sending. Browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request to it, so a forged request from another page looks real to a server that trusts the cookie. SameSite=Strict sends cookies only when the target domain matches the origin, which mitigates it.

sysd-found-060.title: Datagram TLS: security for UDP applications
sysd-found-060.text: TLS runs on a reliable transport such as TCP, but some applications send datagrams instead. Datagram TLS (DTLS) is a protocol based on TLS that secures datagram-based applications against eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery. It is intended to give security guarantees similar to TLS but works with datagram protocols such as UDP, not only stream protocols. Because it preserves the semantics of the underlying transport, an application avoids the delays of stream protocols. It must handle packet reordering, datagram loss and data larger than one datagram. All modern web browsers support DTLS-SRTP for WebRTC.

sysd-found-180.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security: never again without HTTPS
sysd-found-180.text: A site can tell browsers to stop talking to it over anything but HTTPS. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) does this, protecting against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrades and cookie hijacking. A server sets the policy with the Strict-Transport-Security response header, honored only over an HTTPS connection. Its max-age is in seconds, so max-age=31536000 keeps the policy for one non-leap year. While a policy is in effect the browser rewrites insecure links to https before contacting the server. It must end the connection, without letting the user continue, if the connection cannot be secured. This fixes SSL stripping, where an attacker silently turns an HTTPS connection into plain HTTP with no warning. Protection relies on trust on first use: the first visit, and the first request after max-age expires, are unprotected. Browsers ship a preload list of known HSTS sites so that even the first request uses HTTPS, but such a list cannot scale to cover every website. HSTS is ineffective against look-alike or spoofed domains.

sysd-found-074.title: HTTP origins: why the browser checks the certificate matches
sysd-found-074.text: The origin of a URI is the triple of scheme, host and port after normalization. For http, authority belongs to whoever controls the server listening on the port. For https, authority depends on the server's ability to use the private key matching a certificate the client trusts for that origin. A client must verify that the service's identity matches the URI's origin server, to prevent impersonation by an on-path attacker. If the certificate is not valid for the origin, the user agent must get user confirmation or end the connection with a bad certificate error. Ignoring the server's identity leaves the connection open to active attack.

sysd-found-046.title: SSL: the old name that will not go away
sysd-found-046.text: Most major certificate providers still call certificates SSL certificates, although SSL has been deprecated in favor of TLS. SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, is a protocol for encrypting and securing communications on the internet, first developed in 1995. Web data was originally sent in plaintext that anyone who intercepted it could read, and SSL was created to fix this and protect user privacy. By encrypting data between the user and a web server, SSL also stops certain attacks by preventing tampering with data in transit.

sysd-found-052.title: Forward secrecy: keeping old conversations safe from future theft
sysd-found-052.text: Suppose someone records your encrypted traffic today and steals the server's key later. Forward secrecy is the property that keeps a session key safe even if one of the private keys is compromised in the future. Without it, a compromised server private key exposes all future sessions that use its certificate and also any past sessions that were intercepted and stored. Having one of the long-term asymmetric keys used to establish an HTTPS session should not make it easier to derive the short-term session key. Nor should it help decrypt the conversation later. TLS can provide it by requiring ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish session keys, and only the DHE and ECDHE exchanges do. In {{ref:sysd-found-188}} it is mandatory: static RSA and other key exchanges without it are dropped. Many clients and servers are not configured to require it, so without Diffie-Hellman a third party that obtains the server's private key can decrypt all recorded traffic. Session tickets and weak Diffie-Hellman parameters can weaken the forward secrecy a server aims to provide.

sysd-found-055.title: TLS versions: from 1.0 to 1.3
sysd-found-055.text: TLS has gone through versions 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, each defined in an RFC and each revised to address security threats. TLS 1.1 was defined in RFC 4346 in April 2006 and TLS 1.2 in RFC 5246 in August 2008. The newest, {{ref:sysd-found-188}}, came in RFC 8446 in August 2018. It supports 1-RTT handshakes with initial 0-RTT support and mandates perfect forward secrecy through ephemeral keys in the (EC)DH key agreement. It drops insecure or obsolete features, including compression, renegotiation, non-AEAD ciphers and static RSA and static DH key exchanges,. It also encrypts all handshake messages after the ServerHello, including the server certificate.

sysd-found-050.title: The TLS handshake: from hello to a shared secret
sysd-found-050.text:
A TLS connection begins with a short exchange that ends with both sides holding the same secret key. In the TLS handshake, the client and server agree on cipher parameters. The server proves its identity with a certificate, and both derive a shared session key for the secured connection.

The client opens with a ClientHello holding the highest TLS version it supports, a random number, and its suggested cipher suites and compression methods. The server answers with a ServerHello choosing from them, ideally the highest version both support. It usually sends a digital certificate holding its name, the trusted certificate authority that vouches for it, and its public key. The client confirms the certificate is valid before proceeding.

Then the session key is made. In older TLS and SSL the client encrypts a random PreMasterSecret with the server's public key. The server decrypts it with its private key, and both derive the session key from it. Alternatively Diffie-Hellman key exchange, or its elliptic-curve variant, generates the session key with forward secrecy. Both sides compute a master secret from the random numbers and key material. All other key data for the connection, such as the encryption key and MAC key, is derived from it.

Each side finishes by sending a Finished message, authenticated and encrypted, containing a hash and MAC over the previous handshake messages. The other side verifies it, and if any verification fails, the handshake fails and no connection is created. Otherwise data flows over a secure bi-directional channel until the connection closes. The handshake in {{ref:sysd-found-188}} takes one round trip instead of the two earlier versions need. The client guesses the key exchange algorithm and sends public keys for its guesses in the ClientHello.

sysd-found-057.title: Server Name Indication: which site does the client want
sysd-found-057.text: A server hosting several sites must choose a certificate before it knows which site was asked for. Server Name Indication is a TLS extension in which the client names the host it wants in its ClientHello, so the server can send the right certificate. The TLS handshake happens before the application protocol starts. Without SNI, the server must choose right after the ClientHello, and co-hosted name-based virtual servers would share one certificate. Workarounds exist: a wildcard certificate when all virtual servers share a domain, or listing every virtual host name in the subjectAltName extension. SNI sends the host name before the connection is encrypted.

sysd-found-056.title: TLS cipher suites and key exchange methods
sysd-found-056.text: Before protected data flows, the two sides must agree on a key and a cipher. The client presents the cipher suites it supports, and the server picks one it also supports and tells the client. Key exchange methods include RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, elliptic-curve variants, anonymous Diffie-Hellman and pre-shared key. Anonymous Diffie-Hellman does not check who is on the other end and is rarely used because it is open to man-in-the-middle attacks. Only the ephemeral DHE and ECDHE methods provide forward secrecy. HMAC protects integrity for CBC mode block ciphers, while authenticated encryption such as GCM and CCM has an integrated MAC.

sysd-found-188.title: TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things
sysd-found-188.text: TLS 1.3 got better largely by losing features. It is the current version of Transport Layer Security, designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery between client and server applications. It gives a secure channel over any reliable, in-order stream. The server is always verified and the client optionally, data is visible only to the endpoints, and tampering is detected even if an attacker controls the network. TLS has two components, a handshake protocol that checks the parties, negotiates parameters and establishes keys, and a record protocol that protects traffic in independently protected records. Legacy features were pruned. Only AEAD ciphers remain, static RSA and Diffie-Hellman suites are gone so all public-key key exchange gives forward secrecy, and compression and custom DHE groups were removed. The handshake has three phases, key exchange, server parameters and proof of identity, and every handshake message after the ServerHello is now encrypted. If the client's key_share is unacceptable, the server sends a HelloRetryRequest and the client restarts with a suitable one. Key derivation was redesigned around HKDF.

sysd-found-059.title: TLS interception: reading traffic that was encrypted
sysd-found-059.text: TLS interception is decrypting, reading and re-encrypting an encrypted data stream in transit, usually through an interception proxy. The interception software terminates the incoming TLS connection, inspects the HTTP plaintext, and opens a new TLS connection to the destination. Network operators use it to scan for malware that encryption would otherwise hide. It creates risks of its own. Traffic is unencrypted at the interception point, which attracts attackers, and the operator or anyone who gains access to the system can mount man-in-the-middle attacks on users.

sysd-found-058.title: What HTTPS does not protect
sysd-found-058.text: Even over HTTPS, an eavesdropper can still see which server you contacted. HTTPS protects content in transit but leaves some information visible. That includes the server's IP address and port, sometimes the domain name, and the amount and duration of traffic. Addresses and port numbers belong to the underlying TCP/IP protocols. Traffic analysis can infer properties of encrypted traffic, because TLS changes the contents but has minimal impact on size and timing. SSL stripping turns an https link into an http link so the attacker talks in clear with the client, and HTTP Strict Transport Security is the countermeasure.

sysd-found-186.title: Starting an HTTP/2 connection: ALPN, h2 and the preface
sysd-found-186.text: An http or https URI does not say which HTTP versions the server supports. For https the client uses TLS with the ALPN extension and the identifier h2, and both sides must then send a connection preface. Support over cleartext http can only be known out of band, and the h2c Upgrade mechanism is deprecated. The client preface is the 24-octet string PRI * HTTP/2.0 followed by SETTINGS, and the server's first frame is a SETTINGS frame. HTTP/2 over TLS must use TLS 1.2 or higher with the SNI extension.

sysd-found-047.title: Mutual TLS: when the client proves itself too
sysd-found-047.text: TLS usually proves only the server's identity. Mutual TLS, or mTLS, is a mode in which both ends of a connection verify that the other holds the correct private key. The mutual mode requires the user to install a personal client certificate in the browser. In the handshake the server requests a certificate. The client sends it plus a signature made with its private key, which proves it owns the certificate. mTLS keeps traffic secure and trusted in both directions. Systems built from {{ref:sysd-msg-083}} commonly use it to verify each other, in a {{ref:sysd-reliab-131}}.

sysd-found-176.title: Types of TLS certificate: server, client, SAN and wildcard
sysd-found-176.text: Certificates differ in what they identify. A server certificate proves the server is the intended destination. A client certificate verifies the client for access control and usually names a person, though username and password is more common. A Subject Alternative Name (SAN) certificate lists several values, such as DNS names and IP addresses, in its subjectAltName field. SANs are the preferred place for DNS names. A wildcard certificate uses an asterisk so one certificate secures many subdomains, but only one level: *.example.com matches sub1.example.com, not example.com or deeper names. Other kinds include email certificates and code-signing certificates that show binaries were not tampered with.

sysd-found-045.title: Why HTTPS switches to symmetric keys for the data
sysd-found-045.text: HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption only to set up a session key and then switches to symmetric encryption for the data. Once client and server hold the same session key, the encrypted data travels over a secure bi-directional channel using symmetric encryption. There are two reasons for the switch. Asymmetric encryption works only one way, so data the server encrypted for the client could be decrypted by anyone holding the public key. It also adds a lot of mathematical overhead for the server, so it is not suitable for data transmission in long sessions.

sysd-found-051.title: TLS session resumption: skipping the expensive part
sysd-found-051.text: Public-key math is expensive, so TLS lets a returning client skip it. A resumed TLS session reuses the results of an earlier handshake, through a session ID, a session ticket or, in TLS 1.3, a pre-shared key (PSK). With session IDs the server maps the ID to the previously negotiated master secret, and the client sends the ID on reconnecting. With session tickets the server stores its session state in an encrypted and authenticated ticket that the client keeps and presents later. The server then stores no per-session state. Tickets can undermine forward secrecy, because long-lived ticket keys defeat the protection of forward secrecy cipher suites. TLS 1.3 replaces both with one PSK exchange. The server sends a ticket after the handshake, and the client offers it in a later ClientHello. If accepted, its key bootstraps the new connection without a full handshake. A PSK combined with (EC)DHE keeps forward secrecy, while a PSK alone loses it for application data. Servers must not set a ticket lifetime above 604800 seconds (7 days).

sysd-found-189.title: TLS 0-RTT: sending data in the first message
sysd-found-189.text: A returning client can send data in its very first flight, and that speed has a price. TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT) lets a client that shares a pre-shared key (PSK) with the server send application data in its first flight. That saves a round trip at the cost of weaker security. The weakness is that 0-RTT data is not forward secret, being encrypted only under keys derived from the PSK, and nothing guarantees it is not replayed between connections. There are two threats: a network attacker duplicating a flight of 0-RTT data, and one exploiting client retries. The second cannot be prevented in TLS, and any application whose clients retry already needs its own anti-replay defense. Clients cannot know what protection a server has, so they must send as early data only what is safe to replay, as with {{ref:sysd-found-036}}. Servers should ensure early data is accepted at most once, for example with single-use tickets deleted from the server's ticket records on use.

sysd-found-067.title: HTTP conditional requests: act only if nothing has changed
sysd-found-067.text: Two clients edit the same resource, and the second save silently erases the first. That is the lost update problem, and conditional requests prevent it. A conditional request carries header fields that set a precondition to be tested before the method is applied to the target resource. Each precondition compares validators from earlier representations with the current validators. If-Match makes a method conditional on the current entity tag matching, mostly with POST, PUT and DELETE, and a failure gets 412. If-None-Match with * stops an unsafe method such as PUT from overwriting a representation when the client believes none exists. Conditional GET is the most efficient mechanism for HTTP cache updates. There, If-None-Match is the cheap check: if a listed tag matches, the server answers 304 (Not Modified) for GET and HEAD and 412 (Precondition Failed) for other methods. If-Modified-Since makes a GET or HEAD conditional on a newer modification date, and caches build it from the cached Last-Modified value. When several preconditions are present they are evaluated in order: If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, then If-Range.

sysd-found-069.title: HTTP range requests: asking for part of a file
sysd-found-069.text: An interrupted download does not have to start over. A range request asks for only part of a representation, such as the remainder of an interrupted download, by sending a Range header on a GET. A server fulfilling it sends 206 (Partial Content). A single part needs a Content-Range header, and several parts are sent as multipart/byteranges. A server answers 416 (Range Not Satisfiable) when no requested range is satisfiable. It also does so when the client asks for an excessive number of small or overlapping ranges, a potential denial of service attack.

sysd-found-068.title: Validators and entity tags: how HTTP spots a changed resource
sysd-found-068.text: A date is a blunt way to tell whether a resource changed. A validator is resource metadata that can be used in a precondition to make a conditional request, and HTTP defines modification dates and opaque entity tags. An ETag is an opaque quoted string that identifies one representation of a resource. An entity tag can be more reliable than a modification date when one-second resolution is not enough or dates are not consistently maintained. A strong validator changes whenever the observable representation data changes. A validator such as the ETag in a 201 response describes the new representation, so later conditional requests can prevent lost updates.

sysd-found-080.title: HTTP cache validation: asking the origin whether a copy is still good
sysd-found-080.text:
A stale response is not necessarily a wrong one, and a cache can find out cheaply. Validation, or revalidation, is a cache using a conditional request to ask the next server whether a stored response is still valid instead of fetching it in full. A cache validates when it holds responses for a URI but cannot serve them, for example because they are stale. The forwarded request carries preconditions built from the stored response's validators: the Last-Modified timestamp, sent in If-Modified-Since, and the ETag entity tags, sent in If-None-Match. A cache must send stored entity tags and should send the Last-Modified value as well. If-None-Match takes precedence over If-Modified-Since.

The answer decides what happens next. A 304 (Not Modified) answer means the stored response can be updated, using the headers in the 304, and reused, so no content is transferred. A full response means no stored response was suitable, so the cache uses it for the request and may store it. If validation returns a 5xx, the cache may forward it, or act as if the server did not respond and send a stored response where allowed, or retry. A cache can also send a HEAD request to update or invalidate stored GET responses when validators are missing. Each client in a request chain may have its own cache, so an intermediary cache often receives conditional requests from other caches.

sysd-found-083.title: Cache-Control response directives: the origin's instructions
sysd-found-083.text:
Origin servers give caches their orders in a handful of directives. Response directives are instructions from the origin server that tell caches whether and for how long a response may be stored and reused. The max-age directive says the response is stale once its age exceeds the given seconds. The s-maxage directive overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches and also requires them to revalidate once stale. The no-cache directive means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation. The no-store directive means a cache must not store any part of the request or response. It is not a reliable or sufficient privacy mechanism, since compromised caches may ignore it and networks may be eavesdropped.

The private directive means a shared cache must not store the response because it is for a single user, though a private cache may. It controls where a response can be stored, not the privacy of its content. The public directive explicitly marks a response as cacheable, even for a request with credentials. The must-revalidate directive means that once stale a response must not be reused until the origin validates it. This holds even when the cache is disconnected, in which case a cache should return 504 (Gateway Timeout). Servers should use it only when failing to validate could cause incorrect operation, such as a silently unexecuted financial transaction. The proxy-revalidate directive is like it but applies only to shared caches, and no-transform forbids intermediaries from transforming the content.

sysd-found-081.title: HTTP cache invalidation: forgetting what a write made stale
sysd-found-081.text: Invalidation is a cache removing or marking invalid its stored responses for a URI. Unsafe methods such as PUT, POST or DELETE can change state on the origin, so intervening caches must invalidate stored responses to stay current. A cache must invalidate the target URI when it receives a non-error response, with a 2xx or 3xx status, to an unsafe method. It may also invalidate other URIs, such as those in Location and Content-Location, but never when their origin differs from the target URI's. Invalidation is not global: a state-changing request invalidates responses only in the caches it travels through.

sysd-found-078.title: Storing and reusing HTTP cached responses: the two rule sets
sysd-found-078.text: A cache follows one set of rules for what it may store and another for what it may reuse. It must not store a response unless it understands the request method, the status code is final, and the response has no no-store directive. A stored response may be reused only if the target URIs match, the stored method allows it, and the request headers nominated by Vary match. It must also be fresh, allowed to be served stale, or successfully validated. A shared cache must not reuse a response to a request with credentials unless must-revalidate, public or s-maxage allows it.
